title: Silver broke first, gold is below the line, the miners have not caught up
paragraphs: The flight came on Monday. Silver's December futures opened at $64.66 and traded at $61.75 by 7am New York time, about 4.5% lower in a few hours, as Brent went back above $100, Fed hike odds rose and the Hormuz talks stalled (see Silver's Bad Monday). On Wednesday, inflation day, silver broke below its $61.0 support and the gold/silver ratio rose to about 69. The table starts there: by then the damage in silver was already done.

Gold is the bigger story. The same Monday it completed a head-and-shoulders top: the neckline at $4,375 gave way, and the measured target points towards roughly $3,975. The line that decides it is $4,200, and gold closed below it on all three days in the table: $4,157.66, $4,177.50 and $4,142.70. Even Friday's jobs miss, payrolls +29,000 against 90,000 expected and hike odds down from 28% to 15%, did not lift it, because the dollar index held at 101.93.

That is why the desk would not be surprised to see the miners give back more than gold from here. Miners are gold with leverage, and leverage works both ways: if gold travels towards the pattern target, GDX usually falls faster than GLD. It is a view, not a proven signal. Friday even went the other way, with GDX up 1.2% while GLD fell 0.7%, perhaps helped by diesel futures down about 4% since Wednesday, one of a miner's largest running costs. The first confirmation would be miners/gold closing back below Thursday's 0.2266, while gold stays under $4,200.

Risk aversion is the wild card, and it cuts both ways. The yen futures have made a golden cross, the 50-day average above the 200-day, which threatens carry trades, and the midterm calendar has worked against the dollar before: in 9 of the 13 midterm years since 1974 it fell between 30 September and election day. In a sharp flight to safety, gold is often sold first with everything else to raise cash, and miners fall hardest because they are equities too. In March 2020 gold lost about 12% in two weeks and GDX more than 40%, before gold went on to a record within five months as the dollar weakened and rates fell. A first wave could complete the head-and-shoulders target near $3,975, with the miners leading the losses; a second wave, with a weaker dollar into the midterms, a stronger yen and a Fed that cannot hike, could be the final push gold needs, and then the miners' leverage works in their favour. Nobody knows which comes first. The levels will say: $4,200 and $3,975 for gold, 0.2266 for miners/gold.
What to watch: Shanghai reopens on Thursday 8 October with a week of price moves to catch up on. Then US CPI on Wednesday 14 October, the next inflation test for silver at $61 and gold at $4,200.
